narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year grades. Your third-year class ranking was by far the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly 6 among accepted students) signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your peers later in the program. Your first-year ranking in the lowest decile had a similar but smaller effect, reinforcing the pattern of academic difficulty.

Your LSAT score of 34 worked in the opposite direction. While it is below the 37.2 average of accepted students, the model still saw it as a modest positive factor that slightly increased the chance you might pass. Unfortunately, this encouraging signal was not enough to overcome the much larger negative impact of your class rankings.

Given these results, the clearest next step is to focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program before reapplying. Improving your class standing and sharpening your test skills can meaningfully change how future predictions view your likelihood of success.
